newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Commodity markets keep wary eye on funds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Commodity markets keep wary eye on funds.

text.p: Key commodity markets were mostly little changed to a touch firmer on Wednesday as they steadied after a big sell-off by speculative funds that began a week ago.

Prices on Wednesday seemed more responsive to supply/demand fundamentals than to decisions by the fund managers who seemed, a few days ago, to be anxious to dump some of their holdings in a whole range of assets.
Commodities took hits along with equities and bonds.
In Wednesday's commodity markets the flagship industrial metal, copper, edged higher in reaction to news of a further draw on supervised warehouse stocks.

The drop of 5,350 tonnes in London Metal Exchange inventories, after a fall of more than 6,000 on Tuesday, helped the price of LME three-months delivery copper to end in London up $15 at $2,307 per tonne.
Crude oil also firmed to trade at almost $18.25 for a May barrel of the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend after it sank under fund-led selling below $18 recently.
Oil's rebound was helped by news of low U.S. gasoline stocks and of telephone consultations among ministers of OPEC on the way that the value of the barrel has dropped by some $7.00 since January.

Rumblings of that kind within the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries traditionally make would-be sellers of oil futures cautious, as there is an outside chance the cartel might act to tighten excess supply.

Analysts did not think that fundamentals were strong enough to point to a big rally in oil, but they added that, as in the metals market, the funds could suddenly come back in and swing prices one way or another. "Fundamentals still don't look that great but they aren't the only thing that determine prices," said Scott Carter, senior trader at Tosco Petroleum Corp in London.
"As long as the funds don't buy I wouldn't be surprised to see below $18 again. But in the medium term we might settle into a range between $17.50 and the high-$18s," he added.
Funds continued selling of cocoa, which was exempted from the initial sell-off last week then was hit hard on Monday.
The new selling out of New York took London May cocoa futures down by the afternoon close to 970 pounds sterling a tonne from 972 on Tuesday.
